title: Did Troops Cut D.C. Crime?
hook: A new study found the National Guard's deployment in Washington, D.C. had no measurable effect on violent crime — a case study in evaluating public-safety policy with evidence.
key_points: The U.S. National Guard has been deployed in D.C. since August 2025 as part of a federal anti-crime task force.
A new study reported by NPR found the deployment had no measurable effect on violent crime in the city.
Visible shows of force can be politically popular yet hard to tie to actual changes in crime rates.
Evidence-based policy asks whether an intervention works, not just whether it looks decisive.
content_html: The U.S. National Guard has been stationed in Washington, D.C. since August 2025 as part of a federal task force aimed at fighting crime, with its numbers reportedly set to roughly double. NPR reports that a new study examined the effect of that deployment and found no measurable reduction in violent crime in the city. The finding is a useful window into how public-safety policy can be assessed: by asking what actually changed, rather than how forceful the response looked.
extra_html: Deploying troops or police in large, visible numbers is a common response to public worry about crime, and it can be politically popular precisely because it signals decisive action. But a visible show of force is not the same thing as a measured effect on crime rates. According to NPR's reporting, the study compared the period of the deployment against violent-crime trends and concluded the Guard's presence did not move the numbers. The broader civic lesson is about evidence-based policy: well-designed evaluations try to isolate whether an intervention caused a change, separating it from the many other factors that drive crime up or down. That kind of evidence — rather than how a policy is perceived — is what lets citizens and officials judge whether a costly intervention is worth continuing.

flashcards.prompt: What did the study reported by NPR find about the National Guard's deployment in D.C.?
flashcards.back_html: That the deployment had no measurable effect on violent crime in Washington, D.C., even though Guard numbers were set to roughly double.

flashcards.prompt: Why is this study a useful example of evidence-based policy evaluation?

choices.text: It asks whether an intervention actually changed outcomes, not just whether it looked decisive
It proves that no public-safety policy ever works
It shows crime data cannot be measured at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Evidence-based evaluation tests whether a policy produced real effects — a visible, popular response is not the same as an effective one.
